Wiles’s proof begins with a contradiction. Suppose there were positive integers \(a,b,c\) and an exponent \(n>2\) satisfying \(a^n+b^n=c^n\). By elementary reductions, it is enough to consider \(n=4\) or an odd prime exponent \(p\); the case \(n=4\) was already known to be impossible. A hypothetical solution for an odd prime \(p\) would therefore produce a *Frey curve*, an elliptic curve constructed from \(a\), \(b\), and \(c\). This curve is semistable, a condition that restricts its possible types of bad reduction. Building on Frey’s and Serre’s ideas, Ribet proved that the curve arising from such a solution could not be modular. Thus, if every semistable elliptic curve over \(\mathbb Q\) is modular, the hypothetical solution leads to a contradiction. Establishing that modularity statement is the central task Wiles undertook.

The key objects in that task are Galois representations. For a prime \(\ell\), the action of the absolute Galois group of \(\mathbb Q\) on the \(\ell\)-torsion points of an elliptic curve \(E\) gives a residual representation \(\bar\rho_{E,\ell}\). The actions on all \(\ell^m\)-torsion points fit together into an \(\ell\)-adic representation \(\rho_{E,\ell}\). Wiles’s *modularity lifting* strategy was to begin with a residual representation already known to arise from a modular form and, under carefully specified hypotheses, prove that its \(\ell\)-adic lift also arises from a modular form. Applied to the representations attached to \(E\), this establishes the modularity of the elliptic curve. The point is not that one directly matches every torsion representation in turn: a suitable lifting theorem lets information at one chosen prime support a conclusion about \(E\) itself. Its hypotheses, however, are essential; modularity of an arbitrary residual representation alone does not automatically make every lift modular.

Whether the residual representation is reducible or irreducible matters because the main lifting argument requires irreducibility. Wiles used the prime \(3\) where possible: the Langlands–Tunnell theorem supplied the required residual modularity for an appropriate irreducible mod-\(3\) representation. If that representation was reducible, Wiles used a *3–5 switch*, passing to a related elliptic curve to obtain the needed starting point at the prime \(5\). The technical heart of the proof was then a comparison between a deformation ring, which organizes permitted lifts of a residual Galois representation, and a Hecke algebra, which organizes the corresponding modular forms. Showing that these rings agree under the relevant conditions is what turns known residual modularity into modularity of the elliptic curve. Together with Ribet’s theorem, the resulting modularity of semistable elliptic curves rules out the Frey curve—and hence the supposed counterexample to Fermat’s Last Theorem.

For Heidegger, technology is not merely a collection of tools or a means to human ends. It is a way in which beings become intelligible and available to us: a mode of *revealing* (*Entbergen*). He connects this claim to the Greek *alētheia*, often translated as “truth” but understood here as *unconcealment*—the emergence of something from hiddenness into presence. The making of a vessel, for example, brings into view something that was not there before, through the work of materials, form, purpose, and craftsperson. Heidegger associates this kind of bringing-forth with *poiēsis*. Human beings participate in revealing through their practices, but they do not simply manufacture truth at will: any practice of disclosure also depends on a way in which the world already shows itself to them.

Modern technology, Heidegger argues, reveals in a distinctive way. Rather than primarily bringing something forth, it *challenges-forth* nature to supply energy or resources that can be extracted, stored, and ordered. A river encountered as a source of hydroelectric power appears as a resource to be managed; a forest can appear as a stock of timber. Heidegger calls what is disclosed in this way *standing-reserve* (*Bestand*), and he calls the ordering mode of disclosure *enframing* (*Gestell*). This does not mean that technological descriptions are false or that machines alone cause our outlook. The danger is that enframing may become so pervasive that it seems to be the only possible way for anything—including human beings—to appear. Technology thus reveals reality, but its revealing is selective: it brings certain possibilities into view while concealing others.

The distinction between *alētheia* and the later understanding of truth helps clarify the historical stakes of Heidegger’s claim. He associates the Roman *veritas*, and much subsequent thought, with a growing emphasis on correctness: whether a representation accurately corresponds to an object. Heidegger does not deny the importance of correct statements; he asks what prior disclosure makes objects available for representation and judgment in the first place. The passage’s term *destining* (*Geschick*) names the historically given way in which people are set upon a path of revealing—not an unavoidable fate or a decision made by any individual. Technology is therefore “human” insofar as people build, use, and interpret technological systems, yet its essence cannot be reduced to human intention. Recognizing enframing as one historical mode of unconcealment makes it possible to question its dominance and remain open to other ways of encountering the real.

Sexual differentiation of the external genitals and brain occurs through partly overlapping, but not identical, developmental processes. In typical male fetal development, a functional SRY gene initiates testis formation; the testes then produce testosterone and anti-Müllerian hormone. Local conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone is especially important for external genital development. Brain tissues, by contrast, respond to hormones over a longer and region-specific developmental period that extends into postnatal life. Proposed mechanisms for variation in structures such as the central subdivision of the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (BSTc) and the third interstitial nucleus of the anterior hypothalamus (INAH3) include differences in fetal hormone exposure, the timing of that exposure, local steroid metabolism, and androgen- or estrogen-receptor expression and sensitivity. Sex-chromosome genes may also influence neural development directly, rather than acting solely through the gonads. These mechanisms make it biologically plausible for a neural structure and the genitals to follow different developmental trajectories; they do not imply a single, uniform process of “brain sex.”

Prenatal conditions may affect those trajectories, although their effects in humans are difficult to isolate. Variants affecting androgen synthesis or receptor function, and conditions such as congenital adrenal hyperplasia, offer evidence that hormone signaling can influence some later sex-typed behaviors and aspects of identity. Maternal and placental hormone regulation, stress, illness, and exposure to endocrine-disrupting substances have also been investigated. For most such environmental exposures, however, evidence for a specific causal effect on gender identity remains limited or inconsistent. Research on the BSTc and INAH3 is likewise suggestive but not decisive: some postmortem studies report group differences associated with sex or gender identity, yet samples have often been small, and findings must be interpreted in light of overlapping group distributions, hormone treatment, age, and other potential confounders. An adult anatomical difference cannot, by itself, establish when that difference arose or what caused it.

Consequently, the evidence does **not** demonstrate that gender identity is fully “hardwired” before birth. Prenatal biology likely contributes to its development, and the distinction between genital and neural developmental schedules helps explain why anatomy at birth need not predict every aspect of later experience. But gender identity cannot currently be read from the BSTc, INAH3, a gene, or a prenatal hormone measurement. Moreover, *hardwiring* suggests a fixed, one-to-one neural program, whereas brain development involves interacting genetic, hormonal, and environmental processes across time. A more defensible conclusion is that gender identity has developmental biological components whose precise mechanisms, relative contributions, and relationship to particular brain structures remain subjects of research.

La diferenciación genital y la cerebral no ocurren como un único proceso ni necesariamente al mismo tiempo. La formación de los genitales depende, entre otros factores, de la producción fetal de testosterona, su conversión en dihidrotestosterona y la respuesta de los tejidos a los andrógenos durante ventanas tempranas del desarrollo. En el cerebro, las hormonas sexuales también pueden influir sobre la proliferación neuronal, la supervivencia celular, la formación de conexiones y la expresión génica, pero sus efectos dependen de la región y del momento. En modelos animales, la testosterona —y, en algunas especies, su conversión local en estradiol mediante aromatasa— participa en la diferenciación de ciertos circuitos. En humanos, se consideran mecanismos plausibles las variaciones en la exposición prenatal a andrógenos, la sensibilidad de los receptores hormonales y la actividad de enzimas que metabolizan esteroides. También se investigan efectos de los cromosomas sexuales sobre la expresión génica cerebral que no pasan necesariamente por las gónadas. Estas vías podrían, en principio, producir trayectorias parcialmente distintas en el cerebro y en otros tejidos; no se ha establecido, sin embargo, una cadena causal prenatal específica que explique la anatomía adulta del BSTc o del INAH3 en cada persona.

La hipótesis de una diferenciación no concordante entre estructuras se apoya en que los tejidos tienen ventanas de sensibilidad, receptores y programas de desarrollo diferentes. Las variaciones genéticas que afectan a la síntesis hormonal o a la respuesta a andrógenos ofrecen ejemplos claros de cómo la diferenciación corporal puede apartarse de patrones habituales, aunque no permiten inferir directamente una identidad de género individual. Factores del entorno prenatal —como determinadas exposiciones farmacológicas o alteraciones endocrinas materno-placentarias— son asimismo objeto de estudio, pero la evidencia humana que los vincula específicamente con el BSTc, el INAH3 o la identidad de género es limitada. Además, esas estructuras no son marcadores simples de una identidad: algunos estudios post mortem han descrito diferencias de grupo en su tamaño o composición celular, mientras que el número de muestras ha sido pequeño y resulta difícil separar posibles influencias prenatales de los efectos de la edad, las hormonas recibidas a lo largo de la vida y otras experiencias. Tampoco puede suponerse que una medida anatómica adulta reproduzca sin cambios el estado del cerebro fetal.

Por ello, estos hallazgos **no demuestran que la identidad de género esté «cableada» de forma fija y completa antes de nacer**. Sí son compatibles con la idea de que los procesos prenatales contribuyen, junto con el desarrollo posterior, a características neurobiológicas relevantes para la identidad. «Cableado» puede ser una metáfora engañosa: el cerebro se desarrolla mediante interacciones continuas entre genes, hormonas, células y entorno, y conserva plasticidad después del nacimiento. La evidencia disponible tampoco autoriza a reducir la identidad a una región cerebral, a una concentración hormonal fetal o a una única trayectoria de desarrollo compartida por todas las personas trans o cis. La conclusión más sólida es, por tanto, doble: existen mecanismos prenatales biológicamente plausibles para una diferenciación cerebral parcialmente independiente de la genital, pero todavía no conocemos con precisión su contribución causal a la identidad de género humana ni disponemos de una prueba cerebral que determine la identidad de una persona.

```python
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import cosine_similarity

texts = [
    "D'où me vient ce désordre, Aufide, et que veut dire",
    "Madame, il était temps qu'il vous vînt du secours:",
    "Ah! Monsieur, c'est donc vous?",
    "Ami, j'ai beau rêver, toute ma rêverie",
    "Ne me parle plus tant de joie et d'hyménéé;",
    "Il est vrai, Cléobule, et je veux l'avouer",
    "Laisse-moi mon chagrin, tout injuste qu'il est;",
    "Ton frère, je l'avoue, a beacoup de mérite",
    "J'en demeure d'accord, chacun a sa méthode;",
    "Pour prix de votre amour que vous peignez extrême,",
]

# Character n-grams retain information about spelling and word endings.
vectorizer = TfidfVectorizer(
    analyzer="char",
    ngram_range=(2, 5),
    lowercase=True,
    sublinear_tf=True,
)
vectors = vectorizer.fit_transform(texts)

# Cosine similarity measures the angle between each pair of TF-IDF vectors.
similarities = cosine_similarity(vectors)

for i, text in enumerate(texts):
    similarities[i, i] = -1.0  # Exclude the line itself.
    neighbor = similarities[i].argmax()
    print(f"Line {i + 1}: {text}")
    print(f"  Nearest neighbor: line {neighbor + 1}: {texts[neighbor]}")
    print(f"  Cosine similarity: {similarities[i, neighbor]:.4f}")
```

The script represents each literary line as a numerical vector before comparing it with the other lines. Its `TfidfVectorizer` extracts overlapping character sequences of lengths two through five, called *character n-grams*. For example, related forms such as “l’avouer” and “l’avoue” share several sequences even though the complete words differ. Character n-grams are useful for this small corpus because they capture partial spelling correspondences, inflectional endings, and recurring fragments across word boundaries. They can also preserve some evidence of a match when a line contains unusual spelling, such as “beacoup.” Lowercasing makes capitalization irrelevant to the comparison, while punctuation and spaces remain part of the character sequences.

The vectorizer assigns each extracted n-gram a term-frequency–inverse-document-frequency (TF-IDF) weight. Term frequency reflects how often a sequence occurs in a line; inverse document frequency reduces the influence of sequences found in many lines and gives relatively more weight to distinctive ones. The `sublinear_tf=True` option applies a logarithmic adjustment to repeated occurrences, limiting their effect. Because any individual line contains only a small fraction of all n-grams found in the corpus, most entries in its vector are zero. Scikit-learn stores these vectors in a sparse matrix, avoiding the cost of explicitly storing every zero. Fitting the vectorizer to all ten lines establishes one shared feature space, so corresponding vector positions refer to the same n-grams in every comparison.

Cosine similarity then evaluates each pair of vectors using their dot product divided by the product of their lengths. It measures the extent to which two lines emphasize the same weighted n-grams: higher values indicate greater similarity under this representation. The call to `cosine_similarity` produces a matrix in which entry *i, j* compares line *i* with line *j*. Before selecting a neighbor, the script sets each diagonal entry to −1, preventing a line from selecting itself. It then chooses the highest-scoring remaining entry in each row and prints that line and its score. These are nearest neighbors **under the chosen textual measure**, not necessarily lines with the closest literary meaning; the result can change if the n-gram range, weighting scheme, or metric changes.

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.constants import Avogadro, Boltzmann

# Unit conversions for the units specified in the question.
K_B = Boltzmann * 1e21                    # zJ/K
MASS_FACTOR = 1e-3 / Avogadro * 1e21      # (g/mol) -> zJ ps^2/nm^2
PRESSURE_FACTOR = 1e-21 / 1e-27 / 1e5     # zJ/nm^3 -> bar


def integrate(
    N, xyz, v_xyz, L, sigma, epsilon, rc, m, dt,
    tau_T, T_target, tau_P, P_target,
    compressibility=4.5e-5,  # isothermal compressibility, 1/bar
):
    """Advance one velocity-Verlet step with optional Berendsen coupling.

    Set tau_T or tau_P to zero to disable the respective coupling. The
    shifted-force Lennard-Jones interaction is zero in both energy and force
    at rc. Pressure includes its configurational virial.
    """
    xyz = np.asarray(xyz, dtype=float).copy()
    v_xyz = np.asarray(v_xyz, dtype=float).copy()

    if xyz.shape != (N, 3) or v_xyz.shape != (N, 3):
        raise ValueError("xyz and v_xyz must both have shape (N, 3)")
    if min(L, sigma, epsilon, rc, m, dt) <= 0:
        raise ValueError("L, sigma, epsilon, rc, m, and dt must be positive")
    if tau_T < 0 or tau_P < 0:
        raise ValueError("Coupling time constants must be nonnegative")
    if L < 2 * rc:
        raise ValueError("Box side length must be at least twice the cutoff")

    mass = m * MASS_FACTOR

    def forces_and_virial(positions, box):
        forces = np.zeros_like(positions)
        virial = 0.0

        sr_c6 = (sigma / rc) ** 6
        # F_LJ(rc): radial magnitude, positive for repulsion.
        f_cut = 24 * epsilon / rc * (2 * sr_c6**2 - sr_c6)

        for i in range(N - 1):
            for j in range(i + 1, N):
                rij = positions[i] - positions[j]
                rij -= box * np.rint(rij / box)  # minimum image
                r2 = np.dot(rij, rij)
                if r2 >= rc * rc:
                    continue
                if r2 == 0:
                    raise ValueError("Two particles occupy the same position")

                r = np.sqrt(r2)
                sr6 = (sigma / r) ** 6
                f_radial = 24 * epsilon / r * (2 * sr6**2 - sr6) - f_cut
                fij = (f_radial / r) * rij
                forces[i] += fij
                forces[j] -= fij
                virial += np.dot(rij, fij)

        return forces, virial

    # Velocity Verlet: half kick, drift, then half kick.
    forces, _ = forces_and_virial(xyz, L)
    v_half = v_xyz + 0.5 * dt * forces / mass
    xyz_full = (xyz + dt * v_half) % L
    forces, virial = forces_and_virial(xyz_full, L)
    v_xyz_full = v_half + 0.5 * dt * forces / mass

    if tau_T > 0:
        # Remove three translational degrees of freedom if appropriate.
        dof = 3 * N - 3
        if dof <= 0:
            raise ValueError("Thermostat requires at least two particles")
        v_thermal = v_xyz_full - v_xyz_full.mean(axis=0)
        temperature = mass * np.sum(v_thermal**2) / (dof * K_B)
        if temperature <= 0:
            raise ValueError("Cannot thermostat a system with zero temperature")
        lambda_sq = 1 + dt / tau_T * (T_target / temperature - 1)
        if lambda_sq < 0:
            raise ValueError("Thermostat velocity scale would be imaginary")
        v_xyz_full = (
            v_xyz_full.mean(axis=0) + np.sqrt(lambda_sq) * v_thermal
        )

    if tau_P > 0:
        kinetic = 0.5 * mass * np.sum(v_xyz_full**2)
        pressure = (
            (2 * kinetic + virial) / (3 * L**3) * PRESSURE_FACTOR
        )
        volume_scale = 1 - compressibility * dt / tau_P * (
            P_target - pressure
        )
        if volume_scale <= 0:
            raise ValueError("Barostat volume scale must be positive")

        length_scale = np.cbrt(volume_scale)
        new_L = L * length_scale
        if new_L < 2 * rc:
            raise Exception(
                "Berendsen barostat shrank the box below twice the cutoff radius"
            )
        xyz_full = (xyz_full * length_scale) % new_L
        L = new_L

    return xyz_full, v_xyz_full, L
```

The barostat requires an isothermal compressibility, supplied here as the optional `compressibility` argument in inverse bar. Set it to a value appropriate for the simulated material.

The script below treats a book as one fixed-length string. Its unique index is a nonnegative integer: index `0` denotes a book filled entirely with spaces, and the largest valid index is `25^(410 × PAGE_CHARS) − 1`. The page length is a parameter because the premise specifies 410 pages but not how many characters appear on each page.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Usage: ./babel.sh INDEX PAGE [PAGE_CHARS]
# Example: ./babel.sh 123456789 410 3200
exec python3 - "$@" <<'PY'
import sys

ALPHABET = " abcdefghijklmnopqrstuv.,"
RADIX = len(ALPHABET)
PAGES = 410

def fail(message):
    raise SystemExit(f"Error: {message}")

if len(sys.argv) not in (3, 4):
    fail("usage: babel.sh INDEX PAGE [PAGE_CHARS]")

try:
    index = int(sys.argv[1])
    page = int(sys.argv[2])
    page_chars = int(sys.argv[3]) if len(sys.argv) == 4 else 3200
except ValueError:
    fail("INDEX, PAGE, and PAGE_CHARS must be integers")

if RADIX != 25:
    fail("the alphabet must contain exactly 25 distinct characters")
if index < 0:
    fail("INDEX must be nonnegative")
if not 1 <= page <= PAGES:
    fail("PAGE must be between 1 and 410")
if page_chars < 1:
    fail("PAGE_CHARS must be positive")

total_chars = PAGES * page_chars
if index >= RADIX ** total_chars:
    fail("INDEX is outside the range for this book length")

# Character position 0 is the least significant base-25 digit.
# Output only the requested page, without constructing the whole book.
offset = (page - 1) * page_chars
remaining = index // (RADIX ** offset)
characters = []

for _ in range(page_chars):
    remaining, digit = divmod(remaining, RADIX)
    characters.append(ALPHABET[digit])

sys.stdout.write("".join(characters))
PY
```

The combinatorial premise can be made precise by fixing a page length of \(C\) characters and treating every position as an independent choice from an alphabet of 25 symbols. A book then contains \(N=410C\) character positions. For the script’s default \(C=3200\), this gives \(N=1{,}312{,}000\) positions. Since each position has 25 possible contents, the multiplication principle gives exactly \(25^N\) distinct fixed-length books, provided that differences in any character position count as differences between books. Thus the valid indices are the integers from \(0\) through \(25^N-1\), inclusive. This formalization is important: “all possible books” is not a computable indexing scheme until page length, alphabet order, and the treatment of spaces have been specified. Here a space is an ordinary character, so blank-looking pages and trailing spaces are genuine parts of books rather than formatting to be discarded.

The index-to-text map is a base-25 positional representation. In the declared alphabet, the space has digit value 0, `a` has value 1, and the remaining characters follow in the order shown in the code. For character position \(k\), counted from zero at the beginning of the book, the digit is \(d_k=\lfloor I/25^k\rfloor\bmod25\), where \(I\) is the book index. The character at that position is `ALPHABET[d_k]`. This is a little-endian convention: the first character corresponds to the least significant base-25 digit. Leading zero digits in the usual written numeral become trailing spaces in the book, giving every admissible integer exactly one book of length \(N\). Conversely, reading a book’s characters as digits reconstructs its sole index by the sum \(I=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}d_k25^k\). These inverse operations establish a bijection, not merely a repeatable source of random-looking text.

To retrieve page \(p\), the script skips the \((p-1)C\) earlier positions mathematically by integer-dividing the index by \(25^{(p-1)C}\). It then calls `divmod` exactly \(C\) times to obtain that page’s successive digits and characters. Consequently, it does not need to generate or store the preceding pages; it holds only the requested page and the integer arithmetic needed to reach it. The bounds check ensures that the index denotes a book within the chosen finite library. Different values of `PAGE_CHARS` define different libraries and therefore must be held fixed when an index is cited or shared. Finally, an excerpt like the one in the question is a possible substring, but this scheme does not preferentially generate it: most indices yield the same sort of arbitrary punctuation, spaces, and letter sequences because the construction enumerates combinations rather than linguistic texts.

Clause C is the clearest example of a material term whose wording could defeat a customer’s reasonable expectations. It says overdue amounts incur a charge of “one and one-half percent (10.5%) per month.” Those are two different rates: one and one-half percent is **1.5%**, not **10.5%**. The difference is substantial, especially because the charge applies each month to an unpaid balance. A customer reading the words could reasonably expect a 1.5% monthly charge, while the company might later point to the parenthetical figure to demand 10.5%. Placing the higher figure inside what appears to be a clarification of the lower one obscures a material financial obligation rather than stating it plainly.

The opening qualification does not cure that problem. “To the extent the jurisdiction that You are located in allows You to incur late charges” addresses whether a late charge is legally permitted; it does not tell the customer which of the two stated rates applies. Nor does “or the maximum rate allowed by law, whichever is less” resolve the contradiction: the calculation still depends on whether the contractual rate is 1.5% or 10.5% per month. The clause also adds that all fees are non-refundable and payable in advance, making the payment terms particularly consequential. In that setting, an internally inconsistent late-charge provision can mislead a customer about the cost of missing a payment.

Under the doctrine of reasonable expectations, a court assessing a non-negotiable website agreement could conclude that a customer would not reasonably anticipate being charged 10.5% per month after being told, in words, that the rate is one and one-half percent. The drafter controls the language and had the opportunity to state the rate unambiguously. That does **not** mean the entire agreement is automatically void: the outcome would depend on the agreement, applicable law, and how the clause was presented. A court might instead interpret the ambiguity against the drafter or decline to enforce the disputed higher rate. Among the choices, however, C contains the most concrete textual deception: a contradictory numerical statement embedded in a material payment term.

```python
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Standard Lorenz parameters
SIGMA = 10.0
BETA = 8.0 / 3.0
RHO = 28.0

def lorenz(state):
    x, y, z = state
    return np.array([
        SIGMA * (y - x),
        x * (RHO - z) - y,
        x * y - BETA * z,
    ])

def rk4_step(state, dt):
    """Advance one time step using fourth-order Runge–Kutta."""
    k1 = lorenz(state)
    k2 = lorenz(state + 0.5 * dt * k1)
    k3 = lorenz(state + 0.5 * dt * k2)
    k4 = lorenz(state + dt * k3)
    return state + (dt / 6.0) * (k1 + 2.0 * k2 + 2.0 * k3 + k4)

def integrate(initial_state, times):
    trajectory = np.empty((len(times), 3), dtype=float)
    trajectory[0] = initial_state
    for i in range(1, len(times)):
        trajectory[i] = rk4_step(trajectory[i - 1], times[i] - times[i - 1])
    return trajectory

def main():
    dt = 0.01
    times = np.arange(0.0, 40.0 + dt / 2.0, dt)

    trajectory_a = integrate(np.array([1.0, 1.0, 1.0]), times)
    trajectory_b = integrate(np.array([1.0001, 1.0, 1.0]), times)

    # Euclidean separation at every recorded time.
    distance = np.linalg.norm(trajectory_a - trajectory_b, axis=1)
    print(f"Initial separation: {distance[0]:.6g}")
    print(f"Final separation:   {distance[-1]:.6g}")
    print(f"Maximum separation: {distance.max():.6g}")

    fig = plt.figure(figsize=(12, 5))

    ax1 = fig.add_subplot(121, projection="3d")
    ax1.plot(*trajectory_a.T, linewidth=0.6, label="A")
    ax1.plot(*trajectory_b.T, linewidth=0.6, alpha=0.7, label="B")
    ax1.set(xlabel="x", ylabel="y", zlabel="z", title="Lorenz trajectories")
    ax1.legend()

    ax2 = fig.add_subplot(122)
    ax2.semilogy(times, np.maximum(distance, np.finfo(float).tiny))
    ax2.set(
        xlabel="Time",
        ylabel="Euclidean separation",
        title="Sensitivity to initial conditions",
    )
    ax2.grid(True)

    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

A chaotic attractor is a bounded region of phase space toward which nearby solutions evolve, even though individual trajectories on it do not settle into a fixed point or a repeating orbit. For the standard Lorenz parameters, this region has a recognizable two-lobed, butterfly-like geometry. Trajectories spiral around one lobe, pass near its center, and may then travel to the other lobe. The sequence of switches is irregular, but the motion remains confined to an organized geometric structure. The attractor is termed “strange” because its fine-scale structure is intricate rather than a smooth surface. This combination of confinement and irregularity distinguishes chaotic dynamics from both simple periodic motion and unbounded instability.

A phase space trajectory represents the system’s complete state, here the point \((x,y,z)\), as it evolves in time. The two trajectories computed above begin only \(10^{-4}\) units apart in Euclidean distance. Initially they can appear nearly identical, including in a three-dimensional plot, yet their separation can grow substantially as they follow different routes around the attractor. The distance plot makes that divergence easier to see. Growth need not be monotonic: the trajectories can temporarily approach one another, and their separation cannot continue exponential growth indefinitely because both remain in a bounded region. Numerical trajectories therefore illustrate sensitivity to initial conditions over a finite time interval, not an assertion that the solutions themselves become unbounded.

The maximal Lyapunov exponent quantifies the asymptotic average rate at which an infinitesimal perturbation grows along a trajectory of a deterministic system. If \(\Phi^t\) denotes the flow and \(D\Phi^t(\mathbf{x}_0)\) its derivative with respect to the initial state, one definition is \(\lambda_{\max}=\lim_{t\to\infty}t^{-1}\log\lVert D\Phi^t(\mathbf{x}_0)\rVert\), when the limit exists, with the usual choice of matrix norm. Equivalently, one may examine the growth rate of a sufficiently small perturbation in a direction that exhibits maximal long-term growth. A positive maximal exponent means that nearby initial states separate exponentially *on average* while the perturbation remains small. This does not imply randomness: identical initial conditions in the Lorenz equations produce the same mathematical solution. Rather, positive exponential sensitivity limits practical long-term prediction when initial conditions have finite precision. The plotted finite-distance curve demonstrates the phenomenon qualitatively; by itself, it is not a reliable estimate of the asymptotic exponent.

```python
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Standard Lorenz parameters
SIGMA = 10.0
BETA = 8.0 / 3.0
RHO = 28.0


def lorenz(state):
    """Return the time derivative of [x, y, z]."""
    x, y, z = state
    return np.array([
        SIGMA * (y - x),
        x * (RHO - z) - y,
        x * y - BETA * z,
    ], dtype=float)


def rk4_step(state, dt):
    """Advance one fixed-size fourth-order Runge–Kutta step."""
    k1 = lorenz(state)
    k2 = lorenz(state + 0.5 * dt * k1)
    k3 = lorenz(state + 0.5 * dt * k2)
    k4 = lorenz(state + dt * k3)
    return state + (dt / 6.0) * (k1 + 2.0 * k2 + 2.0 * k3 + k4)


def integrate(initial_state, times):
    """Integrate a trajectory at the uniformly spaced times provided."""
    states = np.empty((len(times), 3), dtype=float)
    states[0] = initial_state
    dt = times[1] - times[0]

    for i in range(1, len(times)):
        states[i] = rk4_step(states[i - 1], dt)

    return states


def main():
    dt = 0.01
    times = np.arange(0.0, 40.0 + dt / 2.0, dt)

    trajectory_a = integrate(np.array([1.0, 1.0, 1.0]), times)
    trajectory_b = integrate(np.array([1.0001, 1.0, 1.0]), times)
    distance = np.linalg.norm(trajectory_a - trajectory_b, axis=1)

    print(f"Initial distance: {distance[0]:.6g}")
    print(f"Final distance:   {distance[-1]:.6g}")
    print(f"Maximum distance: {distance.max():.6g}")

    fig = plt.figure(figsize=(12, 5))

    ax1 = fig.add_subplot(121, projection="3d")
    ax1.plot(*trajectory_a.T, linewidth=0.7, label="Initial x = 1.0")
    ax1.plot(*trajectory_b.T, linewidth=0.7, label="Initial x = 1.0001")
    ax1.set(xlabel="x", ylabel="y", zlabel="z", title="Lorenz trajectories")
    ax1.legend()

    ax2 = fig.add_subplot(122)
    ax2.semilogy(times, distance)
    ax2.set(
        xlabel="Time",
        ylabel="Euclidean separation",
        title="Sensitivity to initial conditions",
    )
    ax2.grid(True, which="both", alpha=0.3)

    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

The Lorenz attractor is a geometric object in three-dimensional phase space, whose coordinates are the instantaneous values of \(x\), \(y\), and \(z\). At the standard parameter values, trajectories typically approach a bounded region with two prominent lobes. They circulate around one lobe, pass near the central region, and then circulate around the other in an irregular sequence. This structure is called a *strange attractor*: it attracts nearby trajectories yet has intricate geometry that is not adequately described as a stable point or a periodic orbit. Its folding and stretching continually reorganize nearby sets of states. The resulting pattern is orderly enough to have recognizable overall shape but complicated enough that individual turns cannot be predicted indefinitely from approximate data.

A phase-space trajectory represents the evolving state of one deterministic solution. Because the Lorenz equations specify a unique derivative at each state, two exact trajectories cannot cross at the same phase-space point and subsequently take different paths. Nevertheless, trajectories launched from extremely close—but distinct—points can separate rapidly. In the script, the initial conditions differ only by \(10^{-4}\) in \(x\), and the plotted Euclidean distance is \(\|\mathbf{x}_A(t)-\mathbf{x}_B(t)\|_2\). An interval of pronounced separation demonstrates sensitivity to initial conditions, while later fluctuations reflect the fact that both trajectories remain within the attractor’s bounded region. Thus, distance over a long interval need not increase monotonically. Numerical error also matters in a chaotic system: RK4 reduces local integration error, but no finite-precision computation can preserve agreement between two chaotic trajectories indefinitely.

The maximal Lyapunov exponent formalizes the average asymptotic rate at which an infinitesimal perturbation grows. For a deterministic flow \(\phi^t\), a common definition is \(\lambda_{\max}=\lim_{t\to\infty}t^{-1}\log\|D\phi^t(\mathbf{x}_0)\mathbf{v}_0\|/\|\mathbf{v}_0\|\), where \(\mathbf{v}_0\) is an infinitesimal initial displacement chosen in a direction that realizes maximal growth. When this limit exists, a positive value indicates exponential amplification of small perturbations along typical trajectories and, consequently, a finite practical prediction horizon. The distance plot illustrates this mechanism but does **not** by itself provide a reliable estimate of the exponent: once the two trajectories are no longer close, their separation no longer measures infinitesimal growth. Estimating the exponent ordinarily requires evolving a tangent perturbation or repeatedly renormalizing the displacement between nearby trajectories, then averaging its logarithmic growth over a sufficiently long run.

```python
from rdkit import Chem, DataStructs
from rdkit.Chem import AllChem
import numpy as np

smiles = {
    "Aspirin": "CC(=O)Oc1ccccc1C(=O)O",
    "Caffeine": "CN1C=NC2=C1C(=O)N(C(=O)N2C)C",
    "Ibuprofen": "CC(C)Cc1ccc(cc1)C(C)C(=O)O",
}

molecules = {}
for name, smi in smiles.items():
    mol = Chem.MolFromSmiles(smi)
    if mol is None:
        raise ValueError(f"Could not parse {name}: {smi}")
    molecules[name] = mol

# Adjacency matrices use RDKit atom order. Entries are bond orders:
# 0 = no bond, 1 = single, 1.5 = aromatic, 2 = double.
for name, mol in molecules.items():
    adjacency = Chem.GetAdjacencyMatrix(mol, useBO=True)
    atom_labels = [atom.GetSymbol() for atom in mol.GetAtoms()]
    print(f"\n{name} adjacency matrix (atom order: {atom_labels}):")
    print(adjacency)

# ECFP4 means Morgan radius 2 (diameter 4). A fixed-length, binary
# fingerprint makes the pairwise bit-vector Tanimoto calculation explicit.
names = list(molecules)
fingerprints = {
    name: AllChem.GetMorganGenerator(radius=2, fpSize=2048)
    .GetFingerprint(molecules[name])
    for name in names
}

similarity = np.array([
    [
        DataStructs.TanimotoSimilarity(fingerprints[row], fingerprints[col])
        for col in names
    ]
    for row in names
])

print("\nPairwise ECFP4 Tanimoto similarity:")
print(" " * 12 + "".join(f"{name:>12}" for name in names))
for name, row in zip(names, similarity):
    print(f"{name:<12}" + "".join(f"{value:12.3f}" for value in row))
```

A molecular adjacency matrix encodes the graph underlying a structure: row and column \(i,j\) refer to atoms, and a nonzero entry indicates a bond between them. The script uses bond-order entries rather than a strictly binary adjacency matrix, so single, aromatic, and double bonds remain distinguishable. An ECFP4 fingerprint instead summarizes many *local neighborhoods* of that graph. Morgan fingerprint construction begins with atom identifiers derived from properties such as element, aromaticity, charge, and connectivity. At each iteration, an atom’s current identifier is combined with the identifiers and bond types of its neighbors and hashed to form an identifier for a larger circular neighborhood. Radius two includes neighborhoods extending up to two bonds from each central atom; “ECFP4” names the corresponding maximum diameter of four bonds. Hashing those identifiers into 2,048 positions produces a compact binary vector. Because the vector is finite, different environments can occasionally map to the same bit—a hash collision—and setting a bit does not preserve how many times its environment occurs.

For binary fingerprints \(A\) and \(B\), let \(a\) be the number of bits set in \(A\), \(b\) the number set in \(B\), and \(c\) the number set in both. **Tanimoto similarity**, equivalent here to Jaccard similarity, is \(T(A,B)=c/(a+b-c)=|A\cap B|/|A\cup B|\). Its associated **Tanimoto distance** is \(1-T(A,B)\). Identical bit vectors have similarity 1; vectors with no shared set bits have similarity 0. The printed matrix is symmetric, with ones on its diagonal, because each drug is identical to itself under this representation. Tanimoto measures overlap *relative to the total number of features present*: two molecules sharing ten bits can score differently depending on how many additional bits each contains. Consequently, the score is not a direct percentage of shared atoms, bonds, or pharmacological activity.

In virtual screening, an ECFP4–Tanimoto score is commonly used to rank database compounds against a reference ligand or to select diverse candidates for testing. There is no universal cutoff separating “similar” from “dissimilar.” A threshold around 0.7 is sometimes used as a practical filter for relatively close analogues, but its meaning depends on fingerprint settings, molecular size, the compound collection, and the scientific objective. Higher scores may help identify compounds within an existing chemical series, whereas lower-scoring candidates can be valuable when seeking novel scaffolds. Even close topological analogues can differ substantially in potency, selectivity, solubility, or toxicity; conversely, distinct structures can share a biological mechanism. For that reason, medicinal chemistry interprets these scores alongside assay results, physicochemical properties, structural models, and an assessment of scaffold diversity—not as predictions of therapeutic equivalence.

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.signal import find_peaks

SAMPLE_RATE = 44_100
DURATION = 1.0
NOTES = {"C4": 261.63, "E4": 329.63, "G4": 392.00}

# Each note has a fundamental plus its second and third harmonics.
# log2(n + 1) increases with harmonic number, so these amplitudes decay.
harmonic_amplitudes = {
    n: 1.0 / np.log2(n + 1.0) for n in (1, 2, 3)
}

num_samples = int(SAMPLE_RATE * DURATION)
t = np.arange(num_samples) / SAMPLE_RATE
audio = np.zeros(num_samples, dtype=np.float64)

for fundamental in NOTES.values():
    for harmonic, amplitude in harmonic_amplitudes.items():
        audio += amplitude * np.sin(
            2.0 * np.pi * harmonic * fundamental * t
        )

# Leave headroom and keep the waveform within a conventional audio range.
audio *= 0.95 / np.max(np.abs(audio))

# Window the finite recording to reduce spectral leakage. Correct the
# magnitude for the window's coherent gain so amplitudes remain interpretable.
window = np.hanning(num_samples)
spectrum = np.fft.rfft(audio * window)
frequencies = np.fft.rfftfreq(num_samples, d=1.0 / SAMPLE_RATE)
magnitudes = (
    2.0 * np.abs(spectrum) / np.sum(window)
)

# Keep prominent local maxima, including fundamentals and overtone peaks.
peak_indices, _ = find_peaks(
    magnitudes,
    prominence=0.03 * np.max(magnitudes),
    distance=10,  # bins; prevents nearby leakage lobes being reported twice
)

expected = [
    (harmonic * fundamental, f"{note} harmonic {harmonic}")
    for note, fundamental in NOTES.items()
    for harmonic in (1, 2, 3)
]

print("Detected frequency peaks:")
for index in peak_indices[np.argsort(frequencies[peak_indices])]:
    frequency = frequencies[index]
    label = min(expected, key=lambda item: abs(item[0] - frequency))[1]
    print(f"{frequency:8.2f} Hz  magnitude={magnitudes[index]:.3f}  {label}")
```

The Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) converts a finite sequence of time-domain samples into coefficients associated with discrete frequencies. For samples \(x[n]\), where \(n=0,\ldots,N-1\), its forward form is \(X[k]=\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}x[n]e^{-j2\pi kn/N}\). Each complex exponential acts as a frequency-specific reference: its multiplication with the signal, followed by summation, measures how strongly that frequency is represented. The coefficient’s magnitude describes spectral strength, while its angle describes phase relative to the sampling interval. At a sample rate \(f_s\), bin \(k\) corresponds to \(kf_s/N\) hertz. Here, 44,100 samples span one second, yielding bins separated by 1 Hz. The Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) computes the same DFT coefficients efficiently; it is an algorithm, not a different transform. Because the specified pitches do not generally fall exactly on 1 Hz bin centers, their energy spreads across neighboring bins. The Hann window reduces the resulting spectral leakage before peak detection.

A musical note’s perceived pitch is strongly associated with its fundamental frequency, whereas its **timbre** depends in substantial part on the relative strengths and phases of its spectral components, their evolution over time, and accompanying noise or inharmonicity. Harmonic overtones occur at integer multiples of a fundamental. Thus, C4 contributes components near 261.63, 523.26, and 784.89 Hz; E4 contributes components near 329.63, 659.26, and 988.89 Hz; and G4 contributes components near 392.00, 784.00, and 1176.00 Hz. The script assigns overtone \(n\) an amplitude of \(1/\log_2(n+1)\), producing decreasing strength for the second and third harmonics. This simplified spectral envelope makes the synthesized notes richer than pure sine waves. Real instruments, however, also differ in attack, decay, vibrato, resonances, and breath or bow noise. Notably, G4’s second harmonic and C4’s third harmonic are close together, so their spectral contributions may influence one another in the mixture.

The **time-frequency uncertainty principle**, often called the Gabor limit in signal analysis, expresses a constraint on simultaneous localization: a measurement concentrated into a short time interval cannot also have arbitrarily narrow frequency spread. In common standard-deviation conventions, temporal and frequency spreads satisfy an inequality of the form \(\Delta t\,\Delta f \geq 1/(4\pi)\), although the numerical constant depends on the definitions used. A longer observation interval improves discrimination between nearby steady frequencies but averages over more of a sound’s temporal behavior; a shorter interval better isolates an onset or rapid timbral change but broadens its spectral estimates. The one-second duration here provides nominal 1 Hz FFT-bin spacing, while windowing trades a wider main spectral lobe for weaker sidelobes. Bin spacing should therefore not be mistaken for unlimited ability to resolve two close tones: reliable separation also depends on the window, signal-to-noise ratio, relative amplitudes, and observation duration.
